Generalize production code when examples reveal the rule, while allowing pragmatic larger or smaller TDD steps based on confidence.
Prefer TDD for complex business-rule domains, and consider implement-then-test for simpler data-centric features unless they contain complex rules.

Treat the testing process as iterative rather than a waterfall of techniques; move back and forth among specification-based, structural, property-based, and other techniques as new information appears, using mastery of each technique's goal to choose the order.

Treat judging test boundaries as a core TDD skill — when you must test against a fake instead of a real external service, record it as a known project risk and test against the real service as soon as a meaningful transaction is possible, and keep every fake or stub minimal—implementing only what the test requires.

Use a tracer object (a named dummy that describes its role on failure) to check routing and to double as a design tool for marking a domain concept; when a test has both expectations and assertions, assert that expectations are satisfied first to get the right failure report, and follow a four-step TDD cycle (fail, report, pass, refactor) treating diagnostics as a first-class feature.
Use TDD to control implementation pace, prevent speculative code, obtain quick feedback, and expose design friction early.
Do not treat TDD as mandatory or magical; use it pragmatically where it improves learning, reflection, and productivity.
Justify TDD by its design feedback, steady progress, refactoring prompts, and improved testability rather than as a way to completely test software.

Write the test before the code it tests, treating test-writing as a design activity that clarifies intent, exposes rigid or unfocused designs, and yields a regression safety net; TDD is a serious skill requiring sustained effort, not an automatic technique.

Let the tests guide development—use their contents to stay focused and their feedback to raise quality—because writing tests first without letting them drive the design does not by itself produce good code, and TDD only works fully when adopted as a whole.

Follow the fundamental TDD cycle—write a failing test, write just enough code to pass, then refactor to the simplest implementation—and obey the Golden Rule that you never write new functionality without a failing test.

Design the process to anticipate unanticipated change, because non-routine projects always hold surprises and everyone must keep learning; be aware that TDD's benefits can be crippled by organizational circumstances such as an early design freeze or non-communicating stakeholders.

On a pre-existing (brownfield) system, start TDD safely by automating the build and deploy process and adding end-to-end tests over the areas you must change—beginning with the simplest path through the system—before refactoring, because it is risky to rework code that has no regression tests.

Expect design to emerge from trying to implement it—few people get designs right up front—so get into the critical areas of the code early and allow yourself to change your mind, relying on small steps and the tests to protect you.
Use empirical evidence about TDD cautiously because findings are mixed and may reflect fine-grained steady progress more than test-first ordering.

Keep tests and code clean as you go (it is far easier than recovering from a mess and rot dissipates a team's good intentions); keep each unit test focused on a few classes without a large fixture, and recognize TDD is unforgiving—poor internal quality yields poor tests—so for sustainable TDD tests must be readable as well as correct.
Adjust TDD baby-step size continuously: go small for uncertainty, evolve simplistic learning code, and stop forcing tiny steps when the next move is clear.
Choose or blend TDD schools based on fit: inside-out classicist tests, outside-in mockist tests, and hybrids all use tests to learn about design.
Clarify apparent business-rule inconsistencies with stakeholders before encoding tests or implementation.
Interpret coverage reports through readability and behavior: do not rewrite code solely to appease coverage when it increases cognitive load.
Use examples, stubs, and larger tests according to value: examples may suffice for simple rules, aggregators can be stub-tested, and integrated doubts justify larger tests.
Use larger component tests to gain confidence closer to user behavior, but add them only when their value justifies their extra work.
Design composable components with small classes behind common interfaces and clean construction patterns to improve testability.
After a larger reproduction test identifies the root unit, add a unit-level regression and keep the larger test only if it remains representative.
Test DAO and SQL-query classes directly because queries encode predicates, business knowledge, constraints, and output-domain hazards.
Apply specification, boundary, structural, condition, MC/DC-style, and category-partition reasoning to SQL queries.
Boundary-test SQL predicates with on/off points and cheap in-points, combining cases when it reduces database setup cost without hiding intent.
Use production-like databases when realism matters, but weigh that against in-memory database speed and engine-difference risk.
Use migration or database-management tooling to keep test schema, constraints, indexes, and cleanup aligned with production schema evolution.
System tests should exercise complete user journeys through the application rather than isolated units.
Selenium-style browser tests require DOM knowledge, stable element location, real browser resource cleanup, and commands that mirror browser interactions.
Browser system tests need repeatable environment reset and clean application state before each run.
Use Page Objects to encapsulate page-specific browser logic behind user-action methods that return destination Page Objects when navigation occurs.
Every Page Object should wait for a stable readiness condition before tests interact with the page, with carefully chosen timeouts to avoid flakiness.
Page Objects should return application-level data structures from page extraction and hide HTML details from test methods.
Invest in Page Object infrastructure, base classes, visit methods, setup page objects, and helpers because system tests are expensive initially but cheaper after structure exists.
Keep assertions in test code and page mechanics in Page Objects so Page Objects do not depend on the test framework.
Reuse browser drivers only when it reduces cost without leaking state, and always close them after the suite.
Use distinct Page Object input and output data structures when the form data and displayed data differ.
Use fast setup APIs or helpers for prerequisite data that is not part of the journey under test, but keep test-only APIs and reset backdoors out of production.
Make HTML test selectors stable and meaningful with IDs or test-specific attributes so presentation-only changes do not break behavior tests.
Pass base URL and browser configuration dynamically, and run cross-browser suites in CI when local multi-browser execution is too costly.
Treat flakiness as a trust and productivity problem; diagnose external resources, dirty shared state, timeouts, async waits, concurrency, and test-order dependencies first.

Diagnose end-to-end web-test flakiness by checking for delayed asynchronous requests, dirty application state, or unavailable components, and avoid mystery-guest fixtures whose external content is not visible in the test body.
When an unavoidable external service is unavailable, the suite should clearly report or skip that condition instead of failing as if the product were broken.

Complement verification that software works as specified with validation that it solves the user's real need, and include quality gates in the pipeline for building the right software, not only technically-correct software.

Treat structural testing as a complementary perspective, not superior to specification-based testing; recognize that loops make complete path coverage impractical, and read a variable with no independent MC/DC effect as a signal to restructure the code.

When reasoning about contracts, interpret HTTP 4xx as client-side precondition failures and 5xx as server-side postcondition failures, and remember that class invariants do not apply to static methods.

Grow the system incrementally and iteratively—feature by feature, each an end-to-end slice—keeping it always integrated, working, well-structured, and thoroughly tested, and refining features in response to feedback.

Use empirical feedback in nested loops (pairing, unit, acceptance, standups, iterations, releases), deploying completed work to a production-like environment each cycle and seeking feedback about every aspect as early as possible, because without deployment the feedback is incomplete.

Automate the whole end-to-end build-and-deploy cycle (that also exercises the deployment process), because its steps are error-prone and repeated throughout the software's life, and remember that a deployable build is only the start of release in large or regulated organizations.

Keep code as simple as possible and optimize for reading (developers read far more than they write), refactoring constantly to remove duplication and clearly express intent; making code testable also drives it toward being cleaner and more modular.

Refactor by changing internal structure without changing behavior, applying small safe transformations and re-running the tests after each step; keep refactoring distinct from redesign, but use refactoring techniques to reach a new design incrementally once a redesign is decided.

When code is difficult to test, ask why (not just how); treat the difficulty as an early warning of a design that will also be hard to change, and refactor to fix it while it is still fresh rather than letting the code rot.

Give each developer their own test environment, maintain a single command that reliably compiles, builds, deploys, and tests the application (and only start coding once it works), add functionality a tiny slice at a time handling one failure at a time, and make failure diagnostics verbose and easy to understand.

Perform even significant refactorings incrementally—scale down each change so you never stray more than a few minutes from working code and backtrack if a path fails—and treat refactoring as a design activity that needs all your design skills, considering the dynamic structure of instances and threads as well as the static structure of classes.

Distinguish external quality (meeting users' needs) from internal quality (ease of understanding and change), and deliberately maintain internal quality because it is what lets a team change behavior safely and predictably and minimizes the risk that a change forces major rework.

Focus object-oriented design on the communication between objects rather than the objects themselves, treating the system as a web of collaborating objects whose behavior emerges from their composition.
Identify object roles with abstract interfaces rather than concrete classes, and think about objects in terms of roles, responsibilities, and collaborators.

Split the system into a value world (immutable, identity-free, equal by state) and an object world (identity, mutable state, computational processes), and design objects to be easily pluggable by following common communication patterns with explicit dependencies.
Never commit failing unit tests to the source repository, and expect unit tests to pass soon after they are written.

Remember that the point of a test is to fail—design tests to detect and report errors, avoid failures you cannot diagnose without a debugger, synchronize with the repository frequently so reverting is cheap, keep tests small, focused, and well-named, and above all make them fail informatively.

Follow 'Tell, Don't Ask'—tell objects what to do with explicit, named interactions rather than chaining getters—and query objects sparingly, phrasing any query to ask the real question you want answered in the caller's terms, because queries let information leak out and make the system rigid.

Emphasize how objects communicate over what they are, which yields more, smaller, domain-oriented abstractions; applying 'Tell, Don't Ask' consistently leads to passing behavior (callbacks) into the system rather than pulling data up, giving better information hiding.

To unit-test a command-sending object, replace its neighbours with mocks and set expectations for how it should communicate; use the test to discover the supporting roles it needs as interfaces (interface discovery), and follow the standard mock-test structure while keeping the intention of every test clear.

Use self-describing matchers with an assertThat-style API so failure messages state clearly what went wrong; note that a mock-object test may need no explicit result assertions, that expectations can precisely constrain counts, parameters, ordering, and responses, and that the expectation block should be visually separate from the action-and-assertion code.
Ground the whole approach on two core principles—continuous incremental development and expressive code.

Kick-start a project by building, deploying, and testing a 'walking skeleton'—the thinnest slice of real functionality automatically built, deployed, and tested end-to-end (process as well as system)—before the first feature, because deploying from the start flushes out technical and organizational risks and nothing forces understanding of a process like automating it.

Let the need for end-to-end testing shape the system's design from the start; if full end-to-end testing is initially too hard use temporary stop-gap infrastructure, keep the walking-skeleton design to a broad-brush whiteboard sketch, and remember that ignoring testability early makes the system hard to test and forces risky later change.

Expect incremental development to front-load project stress and start unsettled before settling into routine; keep a sense of direction with a concrete implementation to test assumptions while limiting early structural choices to whiteboard-level decisions, because the walking skeleton flushes out issues while there is still time, budget, and goodwill.

Develop a feature from inputs to outputs—from the external triggering events, through boundary and intermediate objects, to the domain model and out again—rather than starting by unit-testing new domain objects in isolation and hooking them up later, which invites integration problems and wasted work.

Insulate a domain object from other concerns by introducing a listener interface so it reports status in its own terms, and decide whether a collaborator is a dependency (required, injected at construction) or a notification (optional) by asking whether the object can function without it.

Balance the grain of testing—too coarse causes combinatorial path explosion, too fine misses integration problems—and accept that there is no single correct unit-to-integration ratio, so regularly reflect and adapt the strategy, ensuring the confidence to change code is justified.
Value code that is easy to maintain over code that is easy to write, because the most direct implementation can damage maintainability by obscuring the code or introducing hidden dependencies.

Structure functionality into objects, packages, and programs using two heuristics—separation of concerns (gather code that changes for the same reason) and working at higher levels of abstraction—which, applied consistently, push the system toward a ports-and-adapters architecture that isolates the domain from technical infrastructure.

Compose system behavior from well-understood lower-level objects used as building blocks, and organize code into an implementation layer (the graph of objects, describing how) and a declarative layer (small sugar methods describing what)—effectively an embedded domain-specific language—using a different style for each.

Give every object a single, clearly defined responsibility—if you cannot describe what it does without conjunctions like 'and' or 'or', split it—and use a message-passing style between objects but a more functional, side-effect-free style within an object.

Classify an object's peers as dependencies (required services, so pass them at construction), notifications (fire-and-forget listeners the object keeps updated without caring who listens, which must be one-way), or adjustments (peers that tune its behavior); treat these stereotypes as design-thinking heuristics, not hard rules.

Always create a valid object by passing its required dependencies through the constructor, avoiding partial construction that is then finished with setters; initialize notifications and adjustments to safe defaults (a null object or empty collection) to be reconfigured later, since there is no safe default for a dependency.
Make a composite object simpler than the sum of its parts—its API must hide the existence of and interactions between its components and be no more complicated than any one of them.

Prefer context-independent objects with no built-in knowledge of the system they run in, passing in whatever they need about their environment (permanently at construction or transiently per call); this makes relationships explicit and managed in mapping-layer factories, and treat a class using terms from multiple domains as a possible violation.

Use precise information-hiding language when discussing a design to check that each detail is hidden at the level of the nested domain that actually owns it, since encapsulation is almost always good but information can be hidden in the wrong place.

Use writing the test first as a design tool—it forces describing what before how and keeps the right abstraction (unclear test intent means mixed-up concepts), keeps unit tests small in scope (a long test signals too large a component), and forces you to know an object's dependencies before you can construct it for testing.

Break up an object when it becomes too large to test easily or its test failures are hard to interpret, and when a test becomes too complicated to set up consider bundling up some collaborating objects; then unit-test the extracted parts separately.

Take as much care with test code as production code but in its own style (concrete about example values, abstract about how, reading like a declarative description of what is tested), watch for readability smells, and make the test name the first clue to what is tested—naming tests by the feature the object provides, not the method it exercises.

Define explicit types for value concepts in the domain even if they do little (for a self-explanatory model, easy change-tracing, less confusion, and a home for behavior), introducing value and object types by breaking out, budding off, and bundling up.

Prefer on-demand ('pull') design—when an object needs a service, define an interface for it from the client's point of view, mock it in the client's tests, then implement it and follow the chain of collaborators—and use the question 'if this worked, who would know?' to decide when to introduce a new collaborator.

Do not defer cleanup of unstructured exploratory code too long, because the cost arrives when the team can least afford it; sometimes it is better to treat such code as a spike and reimplement it cleanly once you know what to do.

Prefer narrow interfaces (even if you need more of them) driven into existence from the client, avoid meaningless 'Impl' class names by naming an implementation after something specific, and refactor interfaces as well as classes—merging those that represent one concept and distinguishing those that represent different concepts.

Emphasize interfaces over classes because an object's type is defined by the roles it plays; treat a class as an implementation detail, and prefer refactoring to delegation over inheritance when factoring out common behavior.

Adopt a resilient process that assumes people will misunderstand requirements and technologies and includes techniques to discover and recover from errors early, making substantial changes in small safe steps while keeping the system clean and working, because large restructurings tend to lose their way and take unpredictably longer.

When stakeholders want more than can be delivered usefully, deliver a basic working application first and make it more powerful later, and agree a shared domain vocabulary with stakeholders early to avoid confusion.

For end-to-end testing of asynchronous, event-based systems, cope with asynchrony by polling for a visible effect (UI change or log entry) with a timeout, controlling the application and stepping through the scenario (wait for an assertion, then send the next event), and expect these tests to be slower and more brittle so their failures may need interpretation.

When threading prevents a simple synchronous unit test, use an integration test that waits for the code to stabilize and a polling probe that checks for the desired state until satisfied or timed out; step away from the keyboard to visualize structure (e.g., CRC cards), and marshal any UI-state change made from outside the UI thread onto that thread.

Verify that failures are recorded by having an end-to-end test check a log file's contents, and accept running a test in memory instead of against a real resource when that resource is already covered by an end-to-end test and would add irrelevant dependencies or asynchrony.

Treat asynchronous tests as fundamentally different (control returns before the activity completes), coordinate the test carefully with the system, make it wait for success with a timeout to detect failure, ensure every tested activity has an observable effect, and observe the system by sampling its state or listening for its events.

Beware flickering tests (they mask defects and erode the team's culture of quality), make asynchronous tests succeed fast for rapid feedback (listening is quicker than sampling), define timeout values in one place, and do not scatter ad hoc sleeps and timeouts—factor synchronization and assertion into subordinate objects.

Practice outside-in development—start from the external triggering event and work inward one object at a time until you reach a visible effect—using the failing end-to-end test to define the target for the next coding episode.

Because you cannot catch every configuration option, push to exercise as much of the system as possible as early and as often as you can, and match the test environment's configuration to production where it matters, since configuration differences can hide or introduce bugs.

Make implicit behavior explicit before adding features by promoting anonymous or implicit code into a named class, name a class from a description of its responsibility, avoid depending on a UI component from non-UI logic (hard to test and breaks single responsibility), and when an object must hand off work delegate to a collaborator behind an interface passed in at construction.

Prefer method and type names that closely match what they do; treat early clarifying and restructuring as valuable rather than gold-plating (most teams do too little), and when unsure how to break something up further, push on and see where the code takes you, recording the concern as a to-do.

Use the strictness of an expectation to express intent—an exact count for a call that must happen once, a looser count for status updates whose count does not matter—declaring expectations in any convenient order (adding a sequence only when order matters), and weigh whether to express an expected value as a literal or a calculation.

Use a temporary 'null implementation' to defer effort and keep code compiling, and break a dependency loop when wiring collaborators by creating the object with a null listener and attaching the real notification afterwards.

Express intent in an API through intention-revealing operations, package related behavior on the object it belongs to, ship well-structured source with a library to make it easier to work with, and accept a known-bad shortcut only temporarily and with a recorded to-do to fix it.

Grow a component one feature at a time (rather than a big-bang rewrite), making the smallest change that gets a new structure into place; use empty or placeholder implementations to keep code compiling, catch up on deferred structure just before upcoming requirements need it, and expect earlier investment in clean structure to pay off as new features fit in.

Treat consistency of representation as a guideline, not a rule — it is acceptable to use a simpler representation where a richer one looks too complicated, especially for a field private to a small, easily-changed class where the code reads well.

Consolidate several special-purpose notifications into a single state-change notification carrying an immutable snapshot; model state transitions with immutable value objects whose transition methods return new instances, push decision-making down into the value object or enum that owns the knowledge, and extend the test's expectation language with small, descriptively named matchers.

Do not treat any unit as too small to test; prefer to make an illegal condition impossible by design and, where you cannot, throw a dedicated 'Defect' exception for programming errors; replace noisy switch statements with polymorphic dispatch, write tests even for code that seems unnecessary now (to protect against later change), remove now-unnecessary forwarding as the design clarifies, and use small helper methods for readability.

Move comparison and decision logic onto the object that owns the data (avoiding the 'feature envy' smell), which gives a clearer division of responsibilities and lets you change the implementation without changing the collaborator.

Make development progress while user-interface and design details are still being worked out—build to the team's current understanding and keep the code flexible—rather than locking down the whole design before coding.

Keep class responsibilities focused — when a user interaction implies an action outside the UI, the UI class should delegate to a collaborating object, translating framework-internal events into domain events at the boundary and using a listener interface to decouple the source of requests from whatever handles them.

Arrive at a good architecture (such as ports-and-adapters) incrementally by repeatedly adding features and following heuristics while keeping the code clean, and keep the core domain code free of any reference to external infrastructure, with a single entry point binding domain and infrastructure.
When there is no obviously best fix, examine the circumstances and exercise judgment, and be wary that relying on an incidental side effect to fix an issue can cause hard-to-track transient failures.

Expect an agile project's emphasis to shift over time (prove the concept, then reach deployable, then broaden), respond flexibly to changing sponsor needs, extract a new class to gain separation of concerns when one class carries two responsibilities, introduce a role interface to keep top-level wiring simple, and model a new distinct state explicitly when users need information about it.

Handle failures at the boundary—catch everything where a framework silently drops handler exceptions, throw when reading a value that was never set, and keep code that cannot throw outside the try block—being precise about which exceptions to catch except where the outcome is binary and the distinction does not matter.

Prefer giving each object a single responsibility even when it costs more lines of code, letting system behavior emerge from composition, and invent a new collaborator to own a new concern rather than piling it onto an existing class.

Depend on roles (interfaces), not concrete classes; mock concrete classes only as a last resort because subclassing to mock leaves the relationship implicit and overspecifies the client (violating interface segregation), extracting an interface instead forces you to name the relationship. When forced by legacy or unchangeable third-party code, prefer a veneer to direct mocking, never override a class's internal features, and never mock values—just create them.

Prefer composition and dependency injection over getters added only to enable testing, use mock objects to emphasize the roles objects play for each other (mock roles, not objects) and as a design tool for the interfaces between objects, and express expectations through constraint or matcher objects that describe what went wrong.

Diagnose a bloated constructor as one of three things—implicit concept (package arguments used together into a new type), confused object (too many unrelated responsibilities; split it, guided by a confused test suite), or too many dependencies (keep dependencies in the constructor but default notifications and adjustments)—and fix accordingly.

Distinguish support logging (for support staff and operators, driven from real requirements like auditing) from diagnostic logging (programmer scaffolding, off in production); prefer a notification to a support object over inline logging (which mixes concerns), because encapsulating support reporting makes code express intent, centralizes it, and forces a test per report. Treat needing to pass a logger everywhere as a design smell, and remember that excessive logging can itself harm a system.

Use test 'states' with when/then clauses to enforce that invocations happen only in the right state and to model all three participants (object under test, peers, and the test itself), being aware that the first matching expectation wins and that needing combined states and sequences hints something should be broken into simpler pieces.
Treat very liberal, dynamic expectation features as power tools that move testing toward dynamic typing—useful but risky—so use them with care.

Do not couple tests for generic adapter or marshalling code to application domain types (it binds domains, makes tests brittle, and can leave tests silently no longer meaningful); instead test such infrastructure with dedicated 'guinea pig' objects that clearly represent the features exercised.

Make test transaction boundaries explicit rather than rolling back at the end (rolling back never tests commit, cross-transaction interactions, or leaves diagnostic data), extracting transaction management into a subordinate 'transactor' object that runs a unit of work and makes the boundaries stand out.

Bypass an object's public API in a test (e.g., via reflection) only when verifying a tool such as an ORM that itself uses that technique, not when test-driving the object's own design, and in persistence tests ensure referential integrity by persisting referenced entities before saving the entity that refers to them.

Because realistic-infrastructure tests are slow, unit-test your code against a clean domain-defined persistence interface with a mock and verify the real implementation with fine-grained integration tests, organizing all tests into a chain of phases—fast in-memory unit, slower out-of-process integration, and end-to-end—for rapid then incremental feedback.

Recognize that concurrency complicates TDD (weaker confidence, harder diagnosis); decide a broad-brush concurrency architecture ahead of time (often prescribed by frameworks, provable with modeling tools) and then test-drive the objects that fit it, using unit tests for an object's synchronization responsibilities and system tests for whole-system concurrency.

Separate functional concerns from concurrency policy by injecting a task runner or executor, so functional behavior can be unit-tested on the test thread (with a deterministic executor) and the object's API no longer hides its concurrency—treating concurrency as a system-wide concern controlled outside the object (context independence).

Drive out synchronization with stress tests—specify an observable invariant with respect to concurrency, exercise the object from many threads, watch it fail and tune it until it fails reliably, then add synchronization—writing both the functional unit test and the stress test before the code, since without scheduler control you cannot guarantee finding every error.

Stress-test a passive object (threads pass through and mutate its state) by having the test start its own threads and checking that the final state equals what sequential calls would produce, and synchronize the test thread with background threads on a state condition (with a test timeout) rather than a fixed sleep.

When writing a custom matcher, name its factory method so the call site reads clearly and write its description to complete the sentence 'expected <description> but <mismatch-description>' so it fits the frameworks' failure messages.
